1.pericope_label: There was a certain rich man which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods

schools.summary: Concede at the outset that no single parable has been subjected to such various and discordant interpretations, and propose to give a true exposition step by step before surveying the rest. Take the clue from the word steward, already used of the apostles and other ministers as dispensers of divine truths and of the means of grace, and from the apostle who calls himself and his fellow labourers stewards of the mysteries of God: the unjust steward represents primarily the scribes and Pharisees in their teaching and ministerial functions, though the parable is addressed to the disciples, who are called to be stewards too and must give their own account; and the rich man, like the householder of other parables, can be none else than God, who both appoints the stewards and calls them to account. Fix the audience carefully, since the word disciples is not to be restricted to the twelve or the seventy but takes in all the professed followers present, the publicans of the preceding discourse among them, whose danger arose from covetousness or dishonesty. Press the verb of accusation, which occurs only here in the New Testament, means to throw across or back and forth and so to slander by gossip, and implies malice even if the thing said is true, the word for the devil coming of the same root; and observe that the word for wasting is the one used of the prodigal son, so that those who flattered themselves they had not wasted their substance in riotous living are taught that goods may be wasted in other ways. Deny that the reckoning is the day of judgment, since it is a circumstance thrown into the parable to prepare for what follows, and true doctrine is not to be derived from such passages; but hold elsewhere that while the words admit a personal application at the close of any period of trust, their primary sense is the day of judgment of a school or a Church, when its work in the kingdom is done and history passes sentence upon it — and that day was coming fast upon those who heard. Note that the parable is peculiar to this Gospel and hard to explain, that the key is given at the ninth verse, and that the imperative means give back, and give back at once. Add the legal setting from the rabbinic sources, where ground or an olive-yard is let out on condition that the tenant pay a fixed share of the produce, and the parable of the world as a house built, with heaven for its covering, the stars for candles and the fruits of the earth for a table spread, God the owner and man the steward.

State the leading object plainly, that we ought to deal kindly and generously with our neighbours, so that when we come to the judgment seat of God we may reap the fruit of our liberality; and though the parable appears harsh and far-fetched, let the conclusion settle its design. Warn against the method that breeds the discordant readings, since to inquire with great exactness into every minute part of a parable is an absurd mode of philosophising. Deny that alms purchase forgiveness of fraud and extortion and wasteful expenditure, or that they are a sufficient compensation for sensuality, since the first injunction laid on us is to live soberly; but hold that because all the blessings God confers are committed to our administration, our Lord here lays down a method of procedure which will protect us from being treated with rigour when we render our account. Read the calling historically, as made by the prophets sent one after another, by John the Baptist, by Christ himself and by his apostles; and note that the parable, though spoken in the hearing of others, is directed to the disciples with respect to the stewardship they were in.

Account for the place of the parable: having rebuked in three parables those who murmured because He received penitents, our Saviour shortly after subjoins a fourth and a fifth on almsgiving and frugality, because it is the fittest order in preaching that almsgiving should be added after repentance. Then name the erroneous opinion inherent in mankind which increases evil and lessens good, the feeling that all the good things we possess in the course of our life we possess as lords over them and may seize as our especial goods; whereas we are placed in this life not as lords in our own house but as guests and strangers, led whither we would not and at a time we think not of, so that he who is now rich suddenly becomes a beggar. Therefore let every man know himself to be a dispenser of the things of others, whose privileges are granted for a brief and passing use, and cast away from his soul the pride of power and put on the humility and modesty of a steward. Say the same shortly, that we are not ourselves the masters but rather the stewards of the property of others, and that when we manage our wealth not according to our Lord’s pleasure but abuse the trust to our own pleasures, we are guilty stewards. And identify the mammon of the later verses as money, the instigator of unrighteousness and the lord of the whole world, to which the covetous Pharisees were doing servile worship when they derided the sentence that no man can serve two masters.

Read the demand for the account as a demand to produce the books of receipts and disbursements, that the master may see whether the accusation be true or false; or else, taking the original otherwise, simply to give up the business of the stewardship. Explain the office from the Greek, one who superintends domestic concerns and ministers to the support of the family, having the products of the field and the business put into his hands for that purpose. Bring in the rabbinic parallel from Kimchi on Isaiah, that the whole world may be considered as a house builded up, heaven its roof, the stars its lamps, the fruits of the earth the table spread, the owner and builder of the house the holy blessed God, and man the steward into whose hands all the business of the house is committed. And fix the hearers as not only the scribes and Pharisees to whom he had hitherto been speaking but all the younger as well as the elder brethren, the returning prodigals who were now his disciples, so that the teaching is for all who are now in favour with God, and particularly for pardoned penitents, to behave wisely in what is committed to them.

Deny at the outset that the design of Christ’s doctrine was to amuse us with notions of divine mysteries or to entertain us with notions of divine mercies, since the revelation of both in the gospel is intended to engage and quicken us to the practice of Christian duties, and as much as any one thing to the duty of beneficence and doing good to those who stand in need of what we have or can do for them. Ground the exhortation in the reminder that we are but stewards of the manifold grace of God, and that since we have in divers instances been unfaithful and forfeited our Lord’s favour, it is our wisdom to think how we may some other way make what we have in the world turn to good account. And guard the reading: parables must not be forced beyond their primary intention, so that we are not to infer from this one that any person can befriend us if we lie under the displeasure of our Lord.

debates: Whom the unjust steward stands for.
Who the disciples addressed in the opening verse are.
Whether the demand for an account is the day of judgment.
How far the details of a parable may be pressed.
What the verb of accusation implies about the accuser.
outliers: Ellicott calls this the most variously and discordantly interpreted of all the parables.
Barnes denies the reckoning is the last judgment; Ellicott replies that its primary sense is the judgment of a school or a Church in history.
Lightfoot and Clarke independently bring the same parable of the world as a built house from Kimchi.
Robertson and Ellicott both note that the verb of accusation shares its root with the word for the devil.
Tertullian expounds not the opening verse but the mammon of the two masters further down the chapter.
Bede explains the parable’s position as a rule of preaching, almsgiving following repentance.

3.pericope_label: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed — I am resolved what to do — so he called every one of his lord’s debtors

schools.summary: Ask first whether there is not some third thing between digging and begging, and answer from the rabbinic distinction between artificers and labourers: a steward who had conversed only with husbandmen must be supposed skilled in no other handicraft, so that if forced to seek a livelihood he would have to apply himself to digging in the vineyards or fields or olive-yards. Leave the alternative open elsewhere, that he either could not dig, being unacquainted with the business, or would not stoop to so low an employment; and add that it is proper for the sick, the lame and the feeble to beg but not for the able-bodied, and that the most real kindness to a beggar who can work is to set him to work. Read the utterance as character: he has lost the manliness and strength that would have fitted him for actual labour and retains the false shame that makes him prefer fraud to poverty, shuddering at the thought of sitting and asking an alms at a rich man’s door; and apply it to a religious caste or order which, having forfeited its true calling by misuse, has lost the power to prepare the ground for future fruitfulness by the digging that answers to education and the influences lying outside direct religious activity, and which is ashamed to confess its spiritual poverty and own that it is poor and blind and naked. Press the tenses: the infinitive means ashamed to begin to beg, where the participle would mean ashamed while begging; and the aorist of the resolve is a burst of daylight to the puzzled and darkened man, a sudden solution which no English tense reproduces, more literally I know or even I knew, as of a man to whom a plan occurs suddenly. Note that the abruptness leaves it briefly uncertain who they are that will receive him, and that the word for debtor is a late one occurring twice in the New Testament. Judge the debtors more probably tenants paying rent in kind after the common custom of the East than purchasers of wheat and oil, and in the interpretation take them from the Lord’s Prayer, as those who have sinned against God and made no return for the outward blessings they received; whereupon the unfaithful Church or party secures its position by working on their lower nature, neither giving the sense of peace and pardon nor asserting the righteous severity of God’s commandments, but keeping consciences uneasy and trafficking in its absolutions. And draw the moral of the resolve, that a man who has begun in dishonesty does not shrink from pursuing it, being willing to injure his master further in revenge for removal, so that dishonesty leads sooner or later into difficulty while honesty is the path filled with most comfort and peace.

Shut the alternatives: he could not submit to become a common day-labourer, which was both a severe and a base employment, and to beg he was ashamed; and since these were the only honest ways left him of procuring a morsel of bread, and he would submit to neither, he found he must continue the system of knavery to provide for his idleness and luxury, or else starve — woe to the man who gets his bread in this way, for the curse of the Lord must be on his head and on his heart, in his basket and in his store. Put the contradiction sharply: ashamed to beg, but not ashamed to cheat, which was likewise a sense of honour, called honour by men but pride by angels. And gloss the resolve simply, that knowing what to do means being resolved what to do.

Read the soliloquy as the manner of the scribes and Pharisees, and the resolve as a scheme already formed in the head that will secure a maintenance. Then allegorise the debtors two ways: either the Gentiles, greatly indebted to God through sinning against the law and light of nature, into whose houses and affections the Jews found means to introduce themselves until they had leave to build synagogues and set up their worship again; or the Jews themselves, who were under those stewards and tutors and governors, debtors to do the whole law, who by breaking it contracted large debts, and against whom the ceremonial law stood as a handwriting.

debates: Whether the steward could not dig or would not.
Whether any honest course remained open to him.
What the suddenness of the resolve conveys.
Who the debtors of the parable represent.
Whether the debts are purchases or rents paid in kind.
outliers: Lightfoot answers the steward’s dilemma out of the rabbinic distinction between artificers and labourers.
Ellicott has the steward shudder at the prospect of sitting like Lazarus at a rich man’s door, twelve verses before Lazarus appears.
Barnes turns aside from the parable to a rule about almsgiving to the able-bodied.
Wesley reduces the whole soliloquy to a single antithesis between shame and cheating.
Gill offers two incompatible allegories of the debtors and decides between neither.

6.pericope_label: Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty — and how much owest thou? An hundred measures of wheat

schools.summary: Give the liquid measure as about seven and a half gallons on one set of tables, with a marginal figure of about nine gallons and three quarts, and the dry measure as about eight bushels, with a marginal figure of fourteen bushels and a pottle and a third estimate from a modern lexicon; then decline to settle it, since the amount is not material to the proper understanding of the parable. Report elsewhere that the data are uncertain and conflicting, the liquid measure running from one to three gallons up to the highest marginal estimate and the dry measure from thirteen to about ninety-seven gallons, one calculation making it nearly equal to the English quarter. Transliterate both words as Hebrew, put the liquid at between eight and nine gallons, note that it stands here alone in the New Testament and is not the word for a bush elsewhere in the Gospel, and admit that the data are unclear for both. Raise the question of the unequal abatements, that it seems a great inequality for fifty to be remitted in a hundred measures of oil and only twenty in a hundred of wheat, unless the measures of wheat exceeded the measures of oil tenfold, in which case the twenty remitted amounted to two hundred of the smaller measure. Take the bill as written by the debtor and signed by the steward, and therefore binding, but left in the steward’s hands and so alterable without his master detecting it; explain the haste by his expecting to be removed soon, and remark that all of this was wrong. Prefer the plural reading of the better manuscripts, thy documents, as covering the lease, the contract specifying the rent, and probably the memorandum of the due delivery of the annual share of the produce; render it thy writings, thy contracts, thy note; and explain the speed by the secrecy of the arrangement. And carry the fraud into the interpretation: by tempting the debtors with an immediate gain and making them sharers in his frauds the steward took the readiest and most direct means of securing at once their favour and their silence, which answers to the Pharisees just in proportion as they lost the moral force they had once exercised, accommodating their casuistry to the selfishness of their followers, releasing men by their Corban teaching from the obligation of supporting parents, and making perjury easy by artificial distinctions as to oaths.

Identify the liquid measure with the bath and report the estimates without choosing among them, four gallons and a half on one authority, six gallons and a pottle and half a pint on another, seven gallons and two quarts and half a pint on a third, nine gallons and three quarts on a fourth, some making the measure much larger still. Note from the rabbis that these baths were to be mingled with the meal or flour offerings, which shows them intended for the temple service, and that the bath was the measure of oil as the ephah was of wheat, the two being of the same quantity. And keep the second question short, since the debt is owed to the same lord as before.

Preserve the ancient names of the measures rather than translating them, as with the ancient coins: the liquid measure is the bath, the largest Hebrew measure of capacity except the homer, of which it is the tenth part, and equal to the ephah at seven gallons and a half; the dry measure is the cor, the largest of all whether for solids or liquids, equal to the homer as the bath is to the ephah, and holding about seventy-five gallons and five pints. Then complain of the English: what idea can a mere English reader have of the word measure in these two verses, when the original words are not only totally different but the quantity is as seven to seventy-five? The original terms should be inserted in the text and their contents in the margin, and the present marginal reading is incorrect. Describe the bill as the writing in which the debt was specified together with the obligation to pay at stated times, apparently in the debtor’s own hand and probably signed by the steward, which precluded imposition on either part, so that the rewriting was ordered to prevent all appearance of forgery and to cancel the old engagement. And compare a custom still prevailing in the East, where a buyer carrying a running account receives from the seller a daily slip of account which remains in his hands and by which payment is made.

debates: How large the two measures of the parable were.
Whether the size of the measures matters to the parable.
Why the two abatements are of unequal proportion.
Whether the bill is one document or several.
What the fraud corresponds to in the interpretation.
outliers: Five voices give five incompatible values for the same measure, and none of them agree.
Clarke attacks the English word measure for concealing that the two originals stand as seven to seventy-five.
Barnes declines to settle the metrology on the ground that it does not affect the parable.
Lightfoot alone notices that the abatements are of unequal proportion and resolves it from the measures.
Clarke compares an Indian custom of running accounts kept on daily slips.
Ellicott alone identifies the fraud with the Corban rule and the casuistry of oaths.

8.pericope_label: And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely — make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness

schools.summary: Settle first that the commendation is the master’s and not the Saviour’s, being part of the narrative, and that what is praised is the shrewdness and not the dishonesty, since the master could no more approve the conduct as a moral act than he could the first cheating; note that he praised the man although he had himself been wronged a second time, and prefer shrewdly or discreetly to wisely, since the man remained the steward of unrighteousness even while his shrewdness was commended. Take the phrase literally as the steward of unrighteousness, a genitive of the characteristic attribute after the half-Hebrew idiom, the same construction as the mammon of unrighteousness and the unjust judge; and render the comparison for their generation, with a view to their own advantages and the interests of those like them. Hear in it a grave half-veiled indignation, more keenly incisive than if the veil had been withdrawn, since if this world were all there would be a wisdom worthy of praise when a Church or its teachers adapt themselves to men’s passions and interests at the expense of truth, and what makes such action hateful is that by it the children of light transform themselves into the children of this world. Then set the exposition beside its rivals and let the reader judge, listing them: a lesson to the publicans to exact no more than is appointed; a lesson to all Christians to deal leniently with their debtors; a simple example of prudence in things temporal to be reproduced in things eternal; a reading in which the master was ignorant of the collusion; one which finds in the account nothing but the approach of death; one in which the master is Mammon; one in which the steward is the publicans as a class, or Judas, or Pilate, or the Lord himself, or Paul, or the true penitent, or the devil — and conclude that this wild diversity should make any commentator distrustful of what seems to him an adequate and complete exposition. On the word mammon, take it as Syriac in origin, attested also in Punic, common in the Targums for wealth, and possibly the name of a Syrian deity worshipped as wealth personified, which would explain the use of a Syriac word here; offer besides the rendering hurtful mammon, since the root serves also for dealing damage and riches even well got often prove noxious to their owner, or else a mammon of unrighteousness set in contrast to a mammon of righteousness, since the Jews commonly used the word righteousness for charity and almsgiving. And deny expressly that entrance into heaven is being purchased, that idea being wholly foreign to the context; the purpose is that those helped by the money should give a welcome to their benefactors.

Deny that the commender is Christ, though one version renders it our Lord, and make it the steward’s own master; and deny that he is commended for the injustice, which is contrary to the divine nature, but only for the craft and cunning by which he provided himself a maintenance — the man being branded unjust for wasting his lord’s goods, putting false glosses on the Scriptures, despising the honest ways of digging and begging, falsifying accounts, breaking the least of the commandments and teaching men so, and being liberal with another’s property to wrong objects and for a wrong end. Repeat the rule of reading, that to attempt a meaning for every minute circumstance is to act absurdly, since to make donations out of what belongs to another deserves no applause and no man would patiently endure a villain robbing him and giving the remainder away by his own fancy. Reduce the comparison to its point, that ungodly and worldly men are more industrious and skilful in conducting the affairs of this fading life than the children of God are anxious to obtain the heavenly and eternal life, and charge us by it with highly criminal indifference in not providing for the future with at least the earnestness worldly men show for their own interests. Then guard the application: we are not taught to search for defenders or advocates who will throw the shield of their protection around us, but that by acts of charity we obtain favour with God; and it is foolish and absurd to infer that the prayers or approbation of the dead are of service to us, since on that supposition all bestowed on unworthy persons would be thrown away, whereas the Lord looks not to the persons but to the work, so that liberality exercised even toward ungrateful men avails in his sight.

Blame the common English translation, from whose ambiguous and improper phrasing it has been supposed that our blessed Lord commended the conduct of a wicked man, when the word rendered lord simply means the master of the unjust steward, who spoke highly of the address and cunning of his iniquitous servant and no more approved this than he approved the wasting before it. Explain the two classes: the children of this world are such as mind worldly things only without regarding God or their souls, a phrase by which the Jews always designate the Gentiles, while the children of light are illuminated by the Spirit of God and regard worldly things only as they subserve salvation. Say plainly that they are wiser not absolutely, for they are one and all egregious fools, but that they are more consistent with themselves, truer to their principles, and more steady in pursuing their end. Ground the epithet on riches in their deceitfulness, since riches promise much and perform nothing, exciting hope and confidence and deceiving both, and are therefore set in opposition to the true riches which give what they promise; and call it a horrid and blasphemous perversion of our Lord’s words to insinuate that a man who has acquired riches by unjust means may sanctify them and provide himself a passport to the kingdom by giving them to the poor, since ill-gotten gain must be restored to the proper owners, or if they are dead to their successors. Gloss the failing as dying, and let the welcome be given by those of the children of God who have gone before.

Allow that the steward cast out of his stewardship is nevertheless commended, because he provided himself against the future, but warn that we ought not to take the whole for our imitation, since we should never act deceitfully against our Lord in order that out of the fraud itself we may give alms. Explain the riches of unrighteousness as riches only to the unrighteous, who rest in them as their hope and the fullness of their happiness, whereas when the righteous possess these things they have so much money but no riches save the heavenly and spiritual. Correct the misunderstanding by which some seize the things of others and give something to the poor and think they are doing what is commanded: the interpretation must be corrected into giving alms of your righteous labours, for you will not corrupt Christ your judge, and God being the fountain of justice you are not to give alms out of interest and usury. And state the rule of timing: in order that after death they may find something in their own hand, let men before death place their riches in the hands of the poor.

Ask what the word for wisdom signifies here, since the Gentiles call wisdom a virtue and define it as the knowledge of what is and is not to be done, and Scripture says that God by wisdom prepared the heavens; but Scripture also calls the serpent the wisest of animals, where the word means not a virtue but evil-minded cunning, and it is in this sense that the steward is said to have done wisely, that is cunningly and evilly. Suggest too that commended may be meant not as real commendation but in a lower sense, as when a man is commended in slight and indifferent matters and a certain sharpness of wit is admired for the power of mind it draws out. Elsewhere put the positive lesson: Christ taught those who abound in riches earnestly to love the friendship of the poor and to have treasure in heaven, knowing the sloth of the human mind and how those who court riches bestow no work of charity upon the needy; and make the least in which a man may be faithful the mammon of unrighteousness, that is earthly riches, which seem nothing to those who are heavenly wise, a man being faithful in a little when he imparts aid to those bowed down with sorrow.

Define the riches of unrighteousness as those which the Lord has given for the necessities of our brethren and fellow-servants and which we spend upon ourselves; say that it became us from the beginning to give all things to the poor, but that having become stewards of unrighteousness by wickedly retaining what was appointed for the aid of others, we must not remain in this cruelty but distribute to the poor, that we may be received by them into everlasting habitations. And observe that this teaching about the faithful disposal of wealth leads straight to the saying about two masters, since the management of wealth according to God is obtained no otherwise than by the indifference of a mind unaffected towards riches.

debates: Who commends the steward, and for what.
Whether the word rendered wisely means a virtue or a cunning.
What the mammon of unrighteousness is and where the word comes from.
Whether ill-gotten wealth may be sanctified by almsgiving.
Whether the friends made by wealth can admit anyone to heaven.
outliers: Ellicott lists thirteen rival expositions of the parable, in which the steward is variously Judas, Pilate, Paul, the true penitent, our Lord himself and the devil.
Origen finds the word for wisdom used of the serpent in Genesis and concludes it means cunning here.
Lightfoot proposes hurtful mammon as a rendering, from a legal term for damage to another’s estate.
Ellicott reports a suggestion that mammon was a Syrian deity worshipped as wealth personified.
Clarke calls the sanctifying of ill-gotten gain by alms a horrid and blasphemous perversion.
Wesley grants the comparison only by calling the children of this world egregious fools who are at least consistent.

10.pericope_label: He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much — if ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?

schools.summary: Take the maxim as almost universally true, since a man who shows fidelity in small matters will show it in large, and one who will cheat in little things will do so where more is at stake; ground it in ordinary business, where the man trusted in a very little is promoted to large responsibilities and those who embezzle in great sums began with small ones, and call it one of the profoundest sayings of Christ, these verses being the explanation of the parables before them. Identify the least with what men call wealth and most take for the highest good, so that to be faithful in it is to acknowledge that we hold it as stewards and not as possessors and must render an account; and think the warning meant especially for disciples who, coming mostly from the poorer classes, supposed themselves in no danger of worshipping mammon, and meant probably with reference to the traitor among them, since the love of money may operate on a narrow scale as well as a wide, and wrong-doing in the one case tests character not less perfectly than in the other. Name the true riches as the graces of the gospel, the influences of the Spirit, eternal life, set against a worldly wealth that is false and deceitful and not to be trusted; and note that the Greek adjective for true is the one generally characteristic of the fourth Gospel, this being its only occurrence in the first three, with one instance in Paul after his companionship with the evangelist. Refer the last clause to God, since the word man’s is not in the original, the wealth of the world being his and committed to us as his stewards, uncertain and at any moment removable, while what is called our own is the permanent wealth of heaven. Note the variant by which some editors read our own for your own on the authority of two uncials and a father, the confusion arising from a likeness of pronunciation, but hold that the point of the passage calls for the second person. And apply the whole to the ministry, since there is no sadder story than to see a preacher go down by the wrong use of money and be caught in that snare.

Refuse to press the maxims: they are proverbs taken from ordinary practice and experience, and it is quite enough if they are generally true. It will sometimes happen that a deceiver who had disregarded a small gain shall display his wickedness in a matter of importance; nay, many are content to practise simplicity and fidelity in small things in order afterwards to seize all at once on a large profit — as the historian says, fraud establishes confidence in itself in small matters, that when a fit opportunity arrives it may deceive with vast advantage. And yet the statement is not inaccurate, since in proverbs we attend only to what usually happens; so the exhortation stands, that the disciples act faithfully in small matters in order to prepare themselves for fidelity in matters of the highest importance. Explain what makes riches another’s: God does not bestow them on condition that we shall be attached to them, but so gives them that they may not bind us with their chains, since our minds could not be free and disengaged for dwelling in heaven unless we looked on everything in the world as passing; whereas the spiritual riches that relate to a future life are called our own because the enjoyment of them is everlasting. Add the comparison from custom, that men care less about abusing and allow themselves greater liberty in squandering their own property, because they fear no one will find fault with them, but are more cautious and more timid with a thing entrusted to them in charge or in loan, of which they must afterwards render an account. And apply the whole to the disciples, though not without a view to the covetous scribes and Pharisees who were in hearing and were disturbed by it.

Make the maxim a discipline rather than an observation: he who has the genuine principles of fidelity in him will make a point of conscience of carefully attending to even the smallest things, and it is by habituating himself to act uprightly in little things that he acquires the gracious habit of acting with propriety and honour in matters of the greatest concern; whereas he who does not act uprightly in small matters will seldom feel himself bound in cases of high importance — and can we reasonably expect that a man continually falling by little things has power to resist temptations to great evils? Give two reasons why worldly riches are called another’s: first because they belong to God, who has not designed that they should be any man’s portion, and second because they are continually changing their possessors, being in the way of commerce and going in providence from one to another — a property often noted by sacred and profane writers alike, as by the satirist who says that nature will assign no perpetual heir and make the farm neither his nor mine, and by the poet whose stolen purse was mine and is his and has been slave to thousands. Identify what is your own as grace and glory, the only satisfying portion for the soul, which no man enjoys in its plenitude unless he is faithful to the first small motions of the divine Spirit. And press the stewardship on the rich: none of these temporal things are yours, you are stewards and not proprietors, God lodging them in your hands for a season while they remain his property; if your steward used any part of your estate further or otherwise than you direct he is a knave with neither conscience nor honour, and neither have you either one or the other if you use any part of what is in truth God’s otherwise than he directs.

debates: Whether the maxim about small things holds universally.
What the least and the much refer to.
Whether anyone can be faithful in the unrighteous mammon at all.
Whose the wealth called another’s is.
Whether the last clause reads your own or our own.
outliers: Calvin denies the maxim is more than generally true and quotes a historian on fraud that builds credit in small things to defraud in great.
Lightfoot answers the difficulty of being faithful in unrighteous mammon from the case of Zacchaeus.
Lightfoot refers another’s to other men’s goods, against Barnes, Wesley, Clarke and Ellicott, who all refer it to God.
Ellicott suspects a specific warning to Judas behind the saying about small things.
Ellicott notes that the adjective for true here is otherwise confined to the fourth Gospel among the evangelists.
Clarke supports the point from a Latin satirist and an English poet in the same note.

13.pericope_label: No servant can serve two masters — the Pharisees also, who were covetous, heard all these things, and they derided him

schools.summary: Note that the saying about two masters stands in an equally close sequence in the Sermon on the Mount, which shows that it took its place among the axioms of the religious life which our Lord loved to reproduce as occasion called for them; observe that the word for servant here means a household servant and is the only addition to the earlier form of the saying, and conclude that either one evangelist has placed it wrongly or the words were spoken twice, there being no real reason to object to the repetition of a favourite saying. Explain the derision by the covetousness, since they despised a doctrine which showed that with their love of money they could not be the true friends of God; render the verb as turning up the nose, and say that it implies visible rather than audible signs of scorn, the distended nostril and the sneering lip of the Roman satirist’s phrase, a word that forcibly expresses the physiognomy of contempt. Observe that the word for covetous means literally lovers of money, as distinct from more general cupidity, and occurs elsewhere in the New Testament only in Paul, furnishing another instance of community of language between the apostle and the evangelist; and that the imperfect shows them listening all the while the parable was being spoken to the disciples. Add the dramatic detail, that they had stood without comment through the three parables aimed directly at them and broke silence only at the fourth, no words apparently spoken but their eyes and noses and faces eloquent with a fine disdain. Take the self-justifying as an attempt to appear righteous in the sight of men without regard to the heart, the character being drawn more fully in the later parable of the Pharisee and the publican, where the word justified looks back to this. Render the next phrase literally as that which is high or lifted up among men, and note that the word for abomination is the one used of the abomination of desolation and of the altar set up by Antiochus, naming what causes physical nausea and loathing, chosen as the expression of a divine scorn which answered to their derision and was its natural result; and find withering scorn in its use against these pious pretenders.

Put the saying about two masters as a rule of the heart, which will be either wholly taken up with God or wholly engrossed with the world. Translate the verb of derision as strongly as decency allows, since the original will not go into English, and say they treated him with the utmost contempt; explain it by their being lovers of money, so that being wedded to this life and unconcerned for the other they considered him the most absurd and foolish of men and worthy only of sovereign contempt, because he taught that spiritual and eternal things are to be preferred before the riches of the universe — and ask how many thousands are of the very same sentiment to the present day. Then read the self-justifying as an endeavour to make it appear to men that a man may feel an insatiable thirst after the present world and yet secure the blessings of another, reconciling God and mammon and serving two masters with equal zeal; but God knows the heart, and knows them to be alive to the world and dead to God, so that however they are esteemed among men they are an abomination before him. And state the chain the passage makes: the pride by which they justify themselves feeds covetousness, derides the Gospel and destroys the law, all of it illustrated by a terrible example; a man cannot be faithful to God if he trims between God and the world.

Refuse the explanation that Christ was despised because he chose a plain and familiar style and used no swelling words: the evangelist expressly declares the reason to have been that they were lovers of money, entertaining a firm and deep-seated conviction that the rich are happy and that there is nothing better than to increase wealth by every method and guard whatever has been acquired, so that they reject as absurd paradoxes all the sayings of Christ that tend the other way, and anyone who speaks of despising riches or bestowing alms on the poor is regarded as a madman — for which quote the Latin poet who speaks in the person of a covetous man. Then show that Christ does not give way to their disdainful conduct but constantly maintains the authority of his doctrine against their mockery, and make it the duty of all ministers of the Gospel to pursue the same course, meeting ungodly despisers with the dreadful judgment of God. Declare that the hypocrisy with which they deceive the eyes of men will be of no avail at the judgment seat of God: they were unwilling to have it thought that their mockery defended their own case, but this venom breaks out from a concealed ulcer, just as one might tell the mitred prelates of the present day that their hostility to the Gospel arises from the severity with which it attacks their hidden vices. And limit their righteousness to the sight of men, who can see only the outside of things and judge by that.

Give the occasion: Christ had told them not to boast of their own righteousness but to receive penitent sinners and redeem their sins by almsgiving, and they derided the preacher of mercy, humility and frugality — for two reasons, either because he commanded what was not sufficiently profitable, or because he cast blame upon their past superfluous actions. Define the self-justifying: they justify themselves before men who despise sinners as in a weak and hopeless condition but fancy themselves to be perfect and not to need the remedy of almsgiving; and how justly the depth of deadly pride is to be condemned, He sees who will enlighten the hidden places of darkness. Elsewhere in this same place turn aside to the law of marriage, in order to discuss afterwards the forbidding of divorce: some think all marriage sanctioned by God because it is written that what God has joined man must not put asunder, yet the Apostle allows the unbelieving to depart, which shows that the marriage of all is not from God; do not then put away your wife, lest you deny God to be the author of your union, and consider how hard it is to send her away with child, adding to the parent’s disgrace the loss of filial affection.

Add a solemn warning to the parable: you cannot serve God and the world, so divided are the two interests. Then observe that when this was spoken the covetous Pharisees treated the instruction with contempt, and that he warned them that what they contended for as the law was a wresting of its meaning, as he went on to show in a case respecting divorce. And draw the standing lesson, that there are many covetous sticklers for the forms of godliness who are the bitterest enemies to its power, and who try to set others against the truth.

debates: Why the saying about two masters occurs twice in the Gospels.
What the covetousness of the hearers had to do with their derision.
What the verb rendered derided describes.
What is meant by justifying oneself before men.
How severe the word rendered abomination is.
outliers: Robertson allows outright that one evangelist may have placed the saying in the wrong context.
Calvin rejects the theory that Christ was mocked for a plain and unadorned style.
Clarke declines to render the Latin equivalent of the verb into English.
Ellicott traces the word for covetous to a vocabulary shared by Paul and the evangelist.
Calvin turns the rebuke against the prelates of his own century.
The note printed under Eusebius here expounds the verse after this one, and that under Ambrose the verse four ahead.

16.pericope_label: The law and the prophets were until John — it is easier for heaven and earth to pass than one tittle of the law to fail — whosoever putteth away his wife

schools.summary: Take the two renderings of the disputed verb seriously, since the words may be varied into a plainly contrary sense and may denote either the entertainment of the gospel or its persecution: one version has every man breaking into the kingdom by force, another has every man committing violence upon it; admit the first as the received sense of the parallel saying, but prefer the second here on the supposition that the discourse runs on continuously from the rebuke a few verses earlier, and defend that supposition by the manner of the schools, where transitions infinitely obscure and inextricable at first sight have been made plain and coherent by expositors. Note elsewhere that the verb occurs here and in the parallel passage and nowhere else in the New Testament, is rare in late prose, and here plainly means that everyone forces his way into the kingdom — a plea for moral enthusiasm and spiritual passion and energy that some today affect to despise. Call the thing asserted a rush into the kingdom, from which the Pharisees had held aloof, and note that all previous revelations led up to the work of John as his led up to the work of Christ. Soften the word every into many or multitudes, as when we say that everybody is engaged in a piece of business. Then admit the difficulty of the sequence: the saying about heaven and earth seems unconnected with the teaching about the mammon of unrighteousness, and it is possible that some links of the chain have been dropped, though the exposition already given supplies a connection, since the scribes had been tampering with the sacredness of laws that are not of today or yesterday but fixed as the everlasting hills, and are told that their casuistry cannot set those laws aside in any single instance, such as the one immediately following. Say plainly that these verses occur in the other Gospel in a different order and were not improbably spoken at different times, the design here being to reprove men who made great pretensions to external righteousness while really departing from the law. And on the divorce saying be brief: adultery remains adultery, divorce or no divorce, remarriage or no marriage. Finally, make the parable account for the topic, since the doctrine and discipline of divorce which the Pharisees taught, lowering the sacredness of the life of home and ministering to the growing laxity of men’s morals, was precisely what was meant by the steward bidding the debtors take their bill and write fifty or fourscore measures instead of the hundred.

Explain what the law and the prophets were: until John began his ministry these, with the holy writings, were the only Scriptures the Jews had and contained the whole of the revelation granted them, which they wrested and put false glosses upon, so that it was no wonder they derided Christ; and since spiritual things were promised there under the notion of temporal ones, which they did not understand, they might well imagine the doctrine of despising worldly riches contrary to their own books. Compare the two ministries: it is not wonderful that God should now act so powerfully on the minds of men, for he is not, as formerly, seen at a distance under dark shadows, but appears openly and at hand for the establishment of his kingdom — whence it follows that those who obstinately reject the doctrine now are less excusable than those who despised it before. Add the saying about heaven and earth lest it be thought that because the law and the prophets were until John they are now abrogated and of no further use, since heaven and earth might sooner pass away and the whole frame of nature be dissolved. And charge the divorce practice home: they put away their wives for any cause but the right one, upon every trifling occasion and for every little disgust, by which instance is shown how they abused and depraved the law and, so far as in them lay, caused it to fail, while he who was thought to destroy it maintained its purity and spirituality.

Say that the law and the prophets continued to be the sole teachers till John came and first proclaimed the glad tidings of the kingdom, and that whoever wishes to partake of its blessings must rush speedily in, imitating those who take a city by storm, since there remains but a short time before an utter destruction falls upon this ungodly race, as the Romans are about to enter Jerusalem. Insist that the Gospel does not at all destroy the law. And observe of the whole passage that these verses appear to be part of the sermon on the mount and stand in a much better connection there than here, unless we suppose the same discourse was delivered at different times and places, which is very probable.

State the objection an opponent would raise and concede its force: Christ prohibits divorce and, in order to forbid it, makes it unlawful even to marry a woman who has been put away, whereas Moses permitted repudiation and prescribed the bill of divorcement — you see, therefore, that there is a difference between the law and the gospel, between Moses and Christ. To be sure there is. But answer it from the same Gospel, which gives the solution of this very question, that Moses suffered the bill of divorcement because of the hardness of your hearts, but from the beginning it was not so, since He who made them male and female had likewise said that the two shall be one. Elsewhere approach the same subject through the law of marriage, since not all marriage is from God, the Apostle allowing the unbelieving partner to depart; and urge a man not to put away his wife lest he deny God to be the author of his union, nor to drive away the children with the mother.

debates: Whether men press into the kingdom or offer violence against it.
Why the law and the prophets are said to have been until John.
Whether these three sayings belong here at all.
Whether the divorce saying contradicts the permission given by Moses.
What connects the divorce saying to the parable before it.
outliers: Lightfoot alone reads the verb as persecution rather than eagerness, and defends the reading by the method of the Talmudic schools.
Clarke holds that these verses belong to the Sermon on the Mount and stand in a better connection there.
Ellicott admits that links of the chain may have been dropped, then recovers the sequence from his reading of the parable.
Ellicott identifies the Pharisees’ divorce teaching with the steward’s writing fifty for a hundred.
Tertullian grants the difference between Moses and Christ before resolving it.
Clarke dates the urgency of entering the kingdom by the approach of the Roman armies.

19.pericope_label: There was a certain rich man, clothed in purple and fine linen — and there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, laid at his gate, full of sores

schools.summary: Deny that this is a history: an ancient copy prefaces it as another parable, so it is neither an account of two persons who lately lived at Jerusalem, though the Papists still point out the very spot where the rich man’s house stood, nor of any particular rich man such as Saul or Herod, nor of rich men in general, though it describes the character of many of them who take care of their bodies and neglect their souls. Elsewhere take the opposite view, that though some look upon it as a simple parable, the occurrence of the name inclines one rather to consider it the narrative of an actual fact — while granting that this is of little consequence provided the doctrine is understood. Describe what awaits those who neglect the care of the poor and indulge in every kind of gluttony, giving themselves to drunkenness and pleasure while allowing their neighbours to pine with hunger, and cruelly killing with famine those whom they had the means to relieve. Make the dogs the crowning proof: it was enough to prove a hardened cruelty that such wretchedness did not move him to compassion, since had there been a drop of humanity in him he would at least have ordered a supply from his kitchen; but the worst of it is that he did not learn pity even from the animals, who were guided by the secret purpose of God to condemn him by their example. And when strangers or even brute animals supply our place by performing an office that should have been ours, let us take the lesson.

Say there is no evidence for a real history and take it as a parable teaching what may happen, collecting its design from the conversation before it, which had taught the danger of the love of money, the treacherous nature of riches, and the duty of kindness to the poor. Note that the word rendered beggar means only poor, and should have been so translated to keep up the contrast with the rich man, and that the name is Hebrew and denotes a man destitute of help. Trace the purple to the shellfish from which the dye was taken, distinguish the three shades it covered, and identify the fine linen as Egyptian flax, used for wrapping mummies and so fine that it was called woven air; render the last phrase as making merry brilliantly. Note that the perfect passive of the laying implies he had been flung there and left, as if contemptuous roughness were meant, and that the participle for full of sores is a medical word found here alone in the New Testament. Ask what the single personal name in a parable means, and give three answers, each more or less compatible with the others: an actual beggar of that name may have been known to disciples and Pharisees alike; the significance of the name, God is the helper, may symbolise one who had no other help; or, as seems likeliest, it may have been meant as a warning to a rich man of the same name at Bethany. Explain the sequence by the sneer already recorded, since on one side stood men living in the love of money and on the other disciples poor with the poverty of beggars, and identify the section of Pharisees aimed at as those in kings’ houses and soft raiment. Note that Eastern habits made table waste larger than modern European ones, and raise the question whether the dogs intensify the suffering or contrast brute sympathy with human apathy — deciding for the first, since Eastern feeling saw in the dog an unclean beast and a scavenger of the streets, from which the beggar would have shrunk; or elsewhere leave both constructions open. And keep the philological point that the Talmudists contract the longer Hebrew name into the shorter, while suggesting that since the discourse concerns Abraham and Lazarus one might recall Abraham and Eliezer of Damascus, a Gentile by birth and once heir in prospect, shut out by the birth of Isaac and here restored to Abraham’s bosom, as a possible hint of the calling of the Gentiles.

Refuse to decide between parable and history: if it be a parable it is what may be, and if a history it is what has been, and the account is equally instructive in whichever light it is viewed; note that a marginal reading in some manuscripts even supplies the rich man’s name, and that our Lord could have mentioned it but chose to suppress what might have given great offence. Count his being rich as the first part of his sin. Explain the beggar’s name as a contraction meaning the help of God, properly given to a man both poor and afflicted who had no help but from heaven, and say the name is mentioned because his character was good and his end glorious. Then dissent from the reading of unrelieved cruelty: it is likely the beggar’s desire was complied with, since it is nowhere intimated that he was spurned from the gate, and the later request that he be sent with water is a strong intimation that the rich man considered himself under some obligation to him, nor does Abraham glance at any uncharitable conduct. Explain the phrase about the bosom from the custom at Jewish feasts, where of three persons reclining on a couch the one whose head came near the breast of another was said to lie in his bosom. And guess at the man from the other side, that he was very probably a Pharisee and one that justified himself before men, a very honest as well as honourable gentleman, esteemed for encouraging trade by his dress and for his generosity in keeping so good a table.

Connect the example to what went before, since he had just advised the making of friends with the mammon of unrighteousness and was derided for it, and now confirms by an example what he had set before them. Observe that among the heathen the names of poor men are more likely to be known than those of the rich, and that here the poor man is named and the rich man is not, because God knows and approves the humble but not the proud; and that poverty and sickness consumed him at once, so that he might be the more approved. Turn the clothing into an argument: if the wearing of fine and precious robes were not a fault, the word of God would never have expressed this so carefully, for no one seeks costly garments except for vainglory, that he may seem more honourable than others, and no one wishes to be clothed with such where he cannot be seen. Explain the dye as taken from sea shells scraped with a knife and the linen as a white and very fine kind. And denounce the insolence and pride of the wealthy, who are so unmindful of the condition of mankind that, as if placed above nature, they derive from the wretchedness of the poor an incitement to their own pleasure, laughing at the destitute, mocking the needy, and robbing those whom they ought to pity.

Begin with the tense, that it says there was such a man and not that there is, because he had passed away as a fleeting shadow. Then set the covering against what it covered: ashes, dust and earth he covered with purple and silk, or rather ashes and dust and earth bore purple and silk upon them; and as his garments were, so also was his food — from which draw the rule that our clothing should be such as our food is.

Call the love of money a most wicked passion and one not easy to abandon, since when Satan has planted this malady in a man’s soul he next proceeds to blind him and will not permit him to listen to the words of exhortation, lest a way of healing be found for those ensnared by it; and prove the truth of this from the very instance of the men now listening, who were lovers of riches and enamoured of gain and regarded a bare sufficiency with contempt.

Represent the passage as a description of the different state of the good and the bad in this world and the other. Note that we are not told the rich man got his estate by fraud or oppression, but that a man may have a great deal of the wealth and pomp and pleasure of this world and yet perish for ever under God’s wrath, his sin being that he provided for himself only. Note likewise that we are not told he did the poor man any harm, but neither do we find that he had any care for him. And observe that it is often the lot of some of the dearest of God’s saints and servants to be greatly afflicted in this world.

debates: Whether the account is a parable or a history.
Why the poor man is named and the rich man is not.
What is signified by the purple and the fine linen.
Whether the rich man refused the beggar anything.
Whether the dogs relieve the beggar’s misery or increase it.
outliers: Calvin and Wesley take the account for fact; Gill, Lightfoot and Barnes take it for parable; Clarke refuses to decide.
Lightfoot mocks the guides who still show pilgrims the site of a house that never existed.
Clarke denies the rich man refused the crumbs, arguing from his later request that Lazarus be sent to him.
Lightfoot suggests the name recalls Eliezer of Damascus and hints at the calling of the Gentiles.
Ellicott reads the name as a warning aimed at Lazarus of Bethany.
Gregory argues from the mention of the clothing that fine dress is itself a fault.

22.pericope_label: The beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom; the rich man also died, and was buried — and in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments

schools.summary: Enlarge on the carrying: one angel was not sufficient to carry the poor man, but many come, that they may make a joyful band, each angel rejoicing to touch so great a burden and gladly encumbering himself, that so they may bring men to the kingdom of heaven; and he was carried into Abraham’s bosom that he might be embraced and cherished there. Then correct anyone who thinks that bosom something bodily, lest so weighty a matter be treated lightly: no one could be guilty of such folly as to suppose the corporeal bosom of one man able to hold so many souls; it must be understood as a retired and hidden resting-place where Abraham is, called his not because it is his alone but because he is the father of many nations and was placed first, that others might imitate his pre-eminence of faith. Observe that while the two men were below on earth there was one above who saw into their hearts, exercising the poor man by trials to glory and awaiting the rich man by endurance to punishment. Give the principle of the reversal by a figure, that as the most excellent of mirrors returns an image just such as the face set before it, a joyful image of the joyful and a sorrowful of the sorrowful, so the just judgment of God is adapted to our dispositions, and the rich man who pitied not the poor at his gate is not heard when he needs mercy himself. State the gulf as finality, since after death rewards cannot be changed; and explain why the just do not cross it, for though in the goodness of their nature they feel compassion, being united to the righteousness of their Author they are constrained by such great uprightness as not to be moved with compassion towards the reprobate. And describe the place of punishment as a common place in the interior of the earth, shaded on all sides and dark, in which there is a kind of opening stretching downward through which lies the descent of the souls condemned to perdition; or else as set far off without the world, like the prisons of kings placed at a distance, whence it is called the outer darkness.

Note that the Jews held the spirits of the righteous to be conveyed by angels at their death, and that since our Saviour speaks in accordance with that opinion and expressly affirms the fact, it seems as proper to take it literally as the statement that the rich man died and was buried, there being no more improbability in angels attending departing spirits than in their ministering to men on earth. Derive the phrase about the bosom from the practice of reclining at meals, where the head of one lay on the bosom of another, so that it denotes intimacy and friendship; and add that of the three terms in common use among the Jews for the future blessedness this was the most popular, resting on the idea of a great feast in which Abraham was the host, so that to lie in his bosom was to be there as the most favoured guest. Insist that it was the soul and not the body that was borne, and hear the bare mention of burial as a contrast to the angelic escort. Distinguish the words carefully: the term rendered hell is Hades and not Gehenna, the unseen world of the dead and not the final prison of the lost, so that the parable describes an earlier stage of the life after death than the judgment scene elsewhere, with no mention of the Advent of the Judge — and so far as the parable itself goes there is nothing to exclude the thought that the torments might in part have the character of a discipline as well as of retribution. Note that both the place of blessedness and the place of torment lie in the unseen world, that the Jews believed the two close together, and that this detail does not oblige belief but is called for by the picture; and that the word for torments meant first the touchstone by which metals were tested and then the rack used on witnesses. Enumerate what the parable relates of the place: that it is far from the abodes of the righteous, that it is a place of torment, that a great gulf is fixed, that the suffering is great, and that there is no escape. Deny that the conversation is to be supposed literally true, since it was designed to represent the sufferings more clearly. And take the request two ways, as either the old selfish arrogance of a man who still looks on the beggar as one who may be sent hither and thither to do his bidding, or the traces of pride conquered and a cry for mercy at last from lips that had never uttered it.

Sharpen the reversal: as it made the poor man’s affliction heavier to lie before the gate and behold the prosperity of others, so it added to the rich man’s desolation to see the happiness of the beggar, his punishment being made the more intolerable by comparison. Observe that he lifted up his eyes to look on him and not to despise him, since the one was above and the other below; and that it is not said he was in torment but in torments, for he was wholly in them and his eyes alone were left free, that he might be the more tortured by seeing what another had. Say that he died in body but his soul was dead before, having done none of the works of the soul, all the warmth that issues from the love of our neighbour having fled; and that no one is spoken of as ministering to his burial as to the beggar’s, since while he lived pleasantly in the broad road he had many busy flatterers and at his end all forsook him. And report the opinion of some that hell is the passing from the visible to the invisible and the unfashioning of the soul, since so long as the soul of the sinner is in the body it is visible by its own operations, but when it flies out it becomes shapeless.

Insist that the figures are figures: though a history is being related, spiritual things are described under images adapted to our senses, since souls have neither tongues nor fingers, are not liable to thirst, and do not hold such conversations as are here described; our Lord has drawn a picture which represents the condition of the life to come according to the measure of our capacity. Let the general truth be that believing souls, when they have left their bodies, lead a joyful and blessed life out of this world, and that for the reprobate dreadful torments are prepared which our minds can no more conceive than the boundless glory of heaven. Point out from the beggar that we must not pronounce men accursed of God because they drag out a life full of distresses, since in him the grace of God was so hidden by the deformity of his condition that to the eye of the flesh nothing appeared but a curse, while in a body loathsome and full of rottenness there was lodged a soul unspeakably precious. And elsewhere read the passage as prophecy, taking the beggar’s death for the death of Christ, foretold by the prophets, typified by the sacrifices, voluntary and yet necessary, once for all and of eternal efficacy; and the torment for the state the scribes and Pharisees enter at death, who were blind guides in life and have their eyes opened in hell, and for the vengeance on Jerusalem, when a fire was kindled against their land.

Follow the older reading, since an ancient manuscript Bible and the Anglo-Saxon alike have the rich man buried in hell, the manuscripts wanting the stop after the word for burial, so that the sentence runs, the rich man died also and was buried in hell, and lifting up his eyes, being in torment, he saw. Contrast the two funerals, since nothing is said of the beggar’s and he had the burial of a pauper, while the pomp and pride of the other followed him to the tomb — and add that the rich man was doubtless buried with pomp enough, though we do not read of his lying in state, that stupid and senseless pageantry, that shocking insult on a poor putrefying carcass, having been reserved for our enlightened age. And on the appeal to the patriarch, say that it cannot be denied that here is one precedent in Scripture of praying to departed saints, but ask who it is that prays and with what success, and whether anyone who considers this will be fond of copying after him.

debates: Whether the carrying by angels is to be taken literally.
What Abraham’s bosom is.
What the word rendered hell denotes here.
How much of the dialogue between the two is figure.
What the rich man’s request shows about his character.
outliers: Augustine argues at length against a reader who took Abraham’s bosom for something bodily.
Ellicott distinguishes Hades from Gehenna and allows that the torments here might in part be disciplinary.
Barnes takes the angels literally and the conversation figuratively in the same passage.
Wesley finds in the verse the one scriptural precedent for praying to departed saints, and rejects it.
Clarke prefers a reading that attaches the burial itself to hell.
Gill reads the beggar’s death as the death of Christ and the torment as the fall of Jerusalem.

25.pericope_label: Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things — between us and you there is a great gulf fixed — send him to my father’s house

schools.summary: Find it suggestive that the patriarch does not disown the relationship, and hear in the word the same tone of pity and tenderness used by the father to the elder brother in the parable immediately preceding; then make the reminder the cruelty of the verse, since one of the chief torments will be the remembrance of what was enjoyed and of what was done, with nothing else to do, day or night, but to remember what was and what might have been had the life been right. Press the verb, which means to receive back in full what was promised, and note that the evil things are not called the beggar’s own but simply the evil things that came upon him. Compare the pagan arrangement of the region of the dead, with the seat of the blessed on one hand and of the damned on the other and a great river or gulf between, and show that the Jewish schools were not far from it, debating whether paradise and hell stand a handbreadth apart or with a wall between, some saying they are so even with one another that you may see out of the one into the other. Call the scene a picture out of Dante, steep rocks and a deep gorge, flames on one side and the fair garden and the banquet on the other, those bearing the penalty and those reaping the reward within sight and hearing of each other; and insist that no single detail of such a description can be pressed as a literal representation of the unseen world, since what was wanted was the dramatic and pictorial vividness which impresses itself upon the minds of men and could not otherwise be gained. Deny likewise that the righteous would wish to pass over. Explain the gulf as a chasm, a gaping opening, permanently fixed, and say the chasm is there on purpose to prevent communication. Take the number of the brothers as mentioned merely to preserve verisimilitude, not to be spiritualised or given a hidden meaning, and remark that the man did not ask to go himself, knowing his condition fixed. Hear the repeated appeal to the patriarch as father both as the undue trust of his class in descent rather than in the fatherhood of God, and as showing the earlier refusal accepted submissively, with no rebellious defiance and no blasphemous execration such as men have pictured resounding in the realms of darkness. And observe that the petition has been used to justify prayer to the saints, answering that both parties are in the unseen world, that the patriarch makes no effort to communicate with the brothers, and that recognition after death is nevertheless clearly assumed.

Take the word son as used ironically, a sharp and piercing reproof to one who falsely boasted in his lifetime of his descent, so that it is as if pain inflicted by a hot iron wounded his mind when his hypocrisy and false confidence were set before his eyes. Guard the doctrine at once: it is not meant that eternal destruction awaits all who have enjoyed prosperity, since, as an earlier father judiciously observed, poor Lazarus was carried into the bosom of a rich Abraham, to inform us that riches shut the gate of the kingdom against no man, which stands open alike to all who have made a sober use of riches or patiently endured the want of them; what is meant is only that this man yielded to the allurements of the present life. Elsewhere take the word in the flesh only, since he was no part of Abraham’s spiritual seed and did not tread in the steps of his faith, and draw from it that good men have not always good children and that no trust is to be put in birth and parentage. Read the gulf as the permanency of the future state, the boundaries separating the reprobate from the elect never to be broken through, and turn it into an exhortation to return early to the path while there is yet time, lest we rush headlong into an abyss from which it is impossible to rise; but refuse to interpret strictly the words about those who would pass over, since it is certain that none of the righteous entertain any such desire. And dismiss the inference that the dead feel solicitude about the living as sophistry than which nothing more ridiculous can be conceived, since by the same plausibility one might prove that believing souls are not satisfied with the place assigned them.

Take the sonship according to the flesh, and then ask whether it is not worthy of observation that Abraham will not revile even a damned soul — and shall living men revile one another? Explain the receiving of good things as a choosing: the man did choose and accept worldly things as his good and his happiness, and can any be at a loss to know why he was in torments? This damnable idolatry, had there been nothing more, was enough to sink him to the nethermost hell.

Show the man, when all hope had been taken from him, turning his mind to the relations he had left behind, and asking that another be sent because he felt himself unworthy to offer testimony to the truth — since having failed to obtain even to be cooled a little, much less did he expect to be set free to preach it. Say that it is too late for him to begin to be a master when he has no longer time for learning or for teaching. Remark what fearful sufferings are heaped on him, since besides his punishment his knowledge and memory are preserved, so that sinners in punishment may be still more punished, seeing the glory of those they despised and being harassed about the punishment of those they had unprofitably loved. Take the answer as a declaration that the Old Testament is the ground of faith. And meet the objection that the dead have no care for the living: because he said this, it does not follow that he knew what his brethren were doing or what their condition then was, for his care might coexist with entire ignorance, just as we care about the dead although we know nothing of what they do; and the patriarch may have learnt what he knew of the two lives not while they were going on but afterwards, from the beggar’s own telling.

Mark the perverseness, that not even in the midst of his torments does he keep to the truth, since if the patriarch is his father he should not speak of his father’s house as another; and observe that he has not forgotten his real father, who was his ruin. Answer the request by turning it round: your brethren are not so much your care as God’s, who created them and appointed them teachers to admonish and urge them; and by Moses and the prophets are meant the Mosaic and prophetic writings. Prove from history that he who does not hear the Scriptures takes no heed of the dead who rise, since the Jews wished at one time to kill the risen Lazarus and at another laid hands on the Apostles, notwithstanding that some had risen from the dead at the hour of the Cross. And give the principle: every dead man is a servant, but whatever the Scriptures say, the Lord says; so let it be that dead men should rise again and an angel descend from heaven, the Scriptures are more worthy of credit than all, since the Lord of angels and of the living and the dead is their author.

debates: Whether the word son is spoken in tenderness or in irony.
Whether prosperity in this life is itself a mark of reprobation.
How far the picture of the two states may be pressed.
What the rich man’s concern for his brothers shows.
Whether the passage supports prayer to the dead.
outliers: Ellicott hears pity in the word son; Calvin hears a hot iron.
Ellicott declares that no detail of the scene can be pressed as a literal description of the unseen world.
Lightfoot sets the Jewish debate over the distance between paradise and hell beside the pagan geography of the underworld.
Robertson and Calvin both answer the argument for prayer to the saints, and by different routes.
Augustine allows that the rich man may have cared for his brothers while knowing nothing of their state.
Barnes refuses to allegorise the number of the brothers.

28.pericope_label: I have five brethren, that he may testify unto them — they have Moses and the prophets — neither will they be persuaded though one rose from the dead

schools.summary: Refuse to explain the number of the brothers, since the question cannot be answered with certainty and the allusions some have found to the five senses in which the man passed his life, or to the five books of Moses, are simply fantastic; suggest instead a definite number used for an indefinite one, as with the five wise and five foolish virgins or the five talents. Offer two views of the motive and prefer the second: it may have been a selfish fear of reproaches that would aggravate his sufferings, or the stirring of an unselfish anxiety for others, content to bear his own anguish if only his brothers might escape, the latter harmonising better with the humility of the tone in which the request is made. Say that the number is in any case not to be spiritualised, and that the man labours under the delusion that his brothers will believe the testimony of one come from the dead. Explain what they already possess, the writings of Moses and the remainder of the Old Testament, and note that in Jewish usage the historical books are comprehended under the title of the Prophets, and that the phrase follows the manner of synagogue reading, where even the most rude and illiterate person met with these books although he had no copy of them at home. Make the answer a principle of the whole teaching, that the right use of lower knowledge is the condition of attaining the higher and that without it signs and wonders avail little, so that more was denied the scribes because they had been unfaithful in a little; and add that even the heathen have the evidence of nature and are therefore without excuse. Name what was really lacking: not wealth, not poverty, not alms, not influence, but repentance, which the man had thought was for others and not for all. Set the demand for a sign in its Jewish setting and then in a particular one, recalling the ruler who had hoped to see a miracle and had said that John was risen from the dead, and whom that belief brought not one step nearer repentance. And on the last verse point to a fulfilment nearer than the Resurrection, since within a few weeks another Lazarus was sick and did rise from the dead, and that wonder brought about no repentance either, the priests taking counsel to put him also to death — a coincidence of name and fact hardly to be thought accidental, and a sharp discouragement to any effort at communicating with the dead. Close with a numbered summary of the doctrine: that the souls of men do not die with their bodies; that the soul is conscious after death and does not sleep until the resurrection; that the righteous are taken to happiness immediately at death and the wicked consigned at once to misery; and that wealth does not secure its owners from the grave.

Take the brothers for his kinsmen according to the flesh, and venture a conjecture about the number, noting that there were six brothers in all and that the nation was usually divided into priests, Levites and Israelites, of whom the great council consisted and who read the law in order on the sabbath — while admitting that all conjectures are liable to exception. Then state the rule the answer establishes: in the persons named we are reminded that we have received an undoubted rule of life, and that we have therefore no right to expect that the dead will rise to instruct and persuade us, since those men were appointed to instruct their own age with the design that posterity should have the same advantage from their writings; and there is no excuse for the indifference of those who shelter themselves under the pretext that they do not know what goes on beyond this world, which among irreligious men is a wicked saying, or rather a grunting of hogs. Treat the exchange as a personification expressing the feelings of the living rather than the anxiety of the dead: the doctrine is little esteemed and no man submits to hear God speaking in his own manner, but one would have angels descend from heaven, another the dead come out of their graves, another new miracles performed daily to sanction what he hears, another voices from the sky — and if God were pleased to comply with all these foolish wishes it would be of no advantage to them, since he has included in his word all that is necessary to be known. And note that the man contradicts the patriarch, knowing his brethren to be a rebellious and stiffnecked people who would not hear Moses and the prophets for all their outward boasting of them.

Infer from the answer that the brothers were Jewish believers, who had these writings in their hands but did not permit them to influence their lives. Then stage the request as a scene: many are desirous to see an inhabitant of the other world and converse with him — make way, then, here is a damned soul called up from the fire, hear him tell of his torments and utter his regrets; but we cannot see him, since God has in mercy spared us that punishment, and our very nature would fail at the appearance, so that Christ keeps him as it were behind the curtain and holds a conversation with him in our hearing which we have neither faith nor courage to hold ourselves. Reduce the reply to two remarkable propositions: that the sacred writings contain such proofs of a divine origin that though all the dead were to arise to convince an unbeliever, the conviction could not be greater nor the proof more evident than they themselves afford; and that to escape perdition and come at last to glory a man must receive the testimonies of God and walk according to their dictates — which two things show the sufficiency and perfection of the sacred writings. Ask what influence the personal appearance of a spirit could have on an unbelieving and corrupted heart, and answer, none, except to terrify it for the moment and afterwards leave it ten thousand reasons for uncertainty and doubt. And say that being persuaded means truly to repent, which implies an entire change of heart that a thousand apparitions cannot effect, God only being able to work it by applying his word; while the fear of the brothers coming to that place may justly be read as a fear lest their reproaches add to his own torment.

debates: Why five brothers are named.
Whether the request was selfish or unselfish.
What books are meant by Moses and the prophets.
Why a messenger from the dead would not convince.
What the closing sentence points forward to.
outliers: Ellicott calls numerical allegories of the five brothers fantastic; Gill attempts one on the next page of the same catena.
Ellicott prefers the unselfish reading of the request; Wesley takes the selfish one flatly.
Ellicott and Robertson both identify the closing sentence with the raising of Lazarus of Bethany and the plot that followed it.
Clarke stages the parable as a scene with a damned soul called up before the reader.
Calvin dismisses the plea of ignorance about the next world as a grunting of hogs.
Robertson reads the verse as a discouragement to attempts at communicating with the dead.
